column4: The section labels root ء ن ي as the question of whether a time has arrived; this ayah asks أَلَمْ يَأْنِ while believers still have time to humble their hearts at God's remembrance, unlike the closed moment in 89:23.
The question أنى لهم الذكرى repeats the section's wording from 89:23; here a clear messenger had already come, so the shared question makes late recollection a response to rejected warning.
The section invokes 44:13's messenger as the reason remembrance came too late; this next ayah says they turned away from him, specifying the rejection behind that delay.
The section's question أنى له الذكرى returns as فأنى لهم ... ذكراهم; here it is tied to the Hour arriving suddenly, making the remembrance's timing decisive.
After asking what remembrance will avail when the Hour comes in 47:18, this ayah commands knowledge of God and seeking forgiveness, showing the open response that precedes the late hour.

The section's root ء ن ي appears in وأنى, and its image of reaching after what has passed is sharpened by التناوش من مكان بعيد: the people try to attain faith from a far place when punishment is seen.
The section uses 34:52 for an unreachable late grasp; this next ayah says they had disbelieved before and had made guesses about the unseen from far away, explaining why that grasp fails.
The section says the remembrance scene in 79:35 begins with الطامة الكبرى; this is that overwhelming calamity, the event that makes the following recollection belated.
The section's stated root ذ ك ر and its sense of pursuing what is gone meet يَتَذَكَّرُ here: on the day of the great calamity, a person recalls ما سعى, what they strove for.
The section identifies root ق د م with good deeds sent ahead; this command asks each soul to look at ما قدمت لغد, turning the same forward-looking review into a living instruction.
The section's root ق د م links to ما قدمت يداه, but here the review ends in the disbeliever's wish to be dust; the verse makes the section's late regret concrete.
Using the section's stated root ق د م, this ayah says a person will be told what they sent ahead and left behind, spelling out the future review behind “what I sent ahead for my life.”
The section's root ق د م names deeds sent forward; here every soul learns what it قدمت وأخرت, so the verse makes the same accounting apply to each person.
The section's dictionary gloss for root ق د م treats good work as what one sends ahead; this ayah says God records ما قدموا along with their traces, showing that the forwarded work remains recorded.
The section's scene begins when Hell is brought forth and a person remembers too late; this neighboring passage says الجحيم is kindled before the next ayah says each soul knows what it brought.
The section's late accounting scene is paired here with الجنة أزلفت, the Garden brought near; the next ayah completes the scene by saying each soul knows what it brought.
The section's human remembers only when the end arrives; this ayah says علمت نفس ما أحضرت, that each soul knows what it has brought, in the same Judgment sequence as Hell and the Garden.
The section centers a soul's final awareness; this adjacent Judgment scene has the graves scattered before 82:5 says each soul knows what it sent ahead and left behind.
The section imagines looking back at what was sent ahead; here the record is laid open and people find ما عملوا حاضرا, their deeds present before them, giving that review its record-book scene.
The section's delayed wish to have sent good forward is reflected in each soul finding its deeds present; its wish for a far distance from its evil makes the regret sharper.
The section's person remembers what they did at Judgment; here people emerge أشتاتا ليروا أعمالهم, in groups to see their deeds, making the review public and concrete.
The section's regret concerns what was or was not sent ahead; this next ayah specifies that even an atom's weight of good is seen, giving the review in 99:6 its smallest scale.
As a continuation of the deed-review scene related to the section's late awareness, this ayah says even an atom's weight of evil is seen, completing the two-sided accounting.
The section moves from a final crisis to belated remembrance; this ayah says the agony of death brings the truth, matching the moment when reality can no longer be postponed.
The section's soul faces its final encounter; this neighboring Judgment scene brings every soul with a driver and witness, specifying how the person arrives before the account.
The section's regret is a late awakening; this ayah says the person had been heedless and now the covering is removed, so sight becomes sharp only after the chance to act.
The section calls 89:23 a remembrance that comes too late; this ayah names Judgment يوم الحسرة, the Day of Regret, while people remain heedless and do not believe.

The section's image is recollection after the decisive event; here those who forgot the revelation say the messengers brought truth only when its fulfillment arrives, then ask whether they can return.
The section contrasts a still-open time for remembrance with recollection at the arrival of the end; this ayah sets a boundary: faith then will not benefit a soul that had not believed before.
The section shows recognition after the crisis has arrived; Pharaoh says آمنت while drowning, a direct scene of belief voiced at the point when rescue is too late.
The section's late remembrance is answered by this rebuke to Pharaoh: آالآن, “now?”, marks the boundary between a timely response and one made after disobedience is complete.
The section's person remembers only when the final event comes; here people say آمنا بالله وحده when they see punishment, matching the same late turn toward belief.
After the people believe on seeing punishment in 40:84, this ayah says their faith does not benefit them then, stating the closed boundary that the section's question implies.
The section's late voice discovers too late that it should have prepared; this ayah tells people to turn to their Lord and submit من قبل أن يأتيكم العذاب, while action is still possible.
The section's recollection comes after the moment to act; this next ayah urges following revelation before punishment arrives suddenly, making explicit the warning that could prevent such regret.
The section's speaker says “if only I had sent ahead”; this ayah gives another Judgment lament, يا حسرتى على ما فرطت, for having neglected what was owed to God.
As regret develops after 39:56, this ayah imagines the speaker saying that guidance would have made them among the God-conscious, another late recognition of what was missed.
The section's wish cannot recover the past; this ayah makes the same wish explicit as لو أن لي كرة, “if only I had another return,” so the speaker could do good.
The section's remorse follows a warning ignored until too late; this reply says God's signs had already come and were denied, naming the earlier choice behind the regret.
The section depicts a person wishing they had sent something ahead; here death arrives and the person asks رَبِّ ارْجِعُونِ, trying to return before the resurrection.
The section itself cites this answer to the dying person's request: let me return to do صالح work; كَلَّا and the intervening barrier make the missed chance final.

The section's root ق د م frames good work as provision sent ahead; this ayah urges spending before death and gives the same kind of last-minute plea for more time to give charity and become righteous.
After the plea for delay in 63:10, this ayah says God will not postpone a soul once its term arrives, making the time boundary in the section explicit.

The section's regret is spoken only after judgment begins; here wrongdoers lower their heads before their Lord and ask to be sent back so they can act righteously, exactly the impossible wish the section describes.
The section links late recollection to a missed meeting with God; this ayah answers the earlier request to return by naming their having forgotten that day's meeting.
The section's “if only” comes after the decisive event; here people facing the Fire wish to be returned so they would not deny God's signs, a matching late plea.

The section's regret cannot undo what preceded it; this next ayah says that even if the deniers were returned, they would repeat what they had been forbidden to do, exposing the wish as no real remedy.

The section's speaker wishes they had prepared before the Day; here the wrongdoer bites his hands and says يَا لَيْتَنِي اتَّخَذْتُ مَعَ الرَّسُولِ سَبِيلًا, wishing he had taken a path with the Messenger.
The regret scene in 25:27 continues as a wish not to have taken a particular companion; this adds the specific relationship the wrongdoer blames for the missed path.
The section's wording recalls ذ ك ر as remembrance; here the speaker says the companion turned him away from الذكر after it had come, specifying what was lost before the regret.
The section's “if only” is spoken at the reckoning; here the person given the record in the left hand says يَا لَيْتَنِي لَمْ أُوتَ كِتَابِيَهْ, another regret after the outcome is known.
Following the wish not to have received the record in 69:25, this ayah says the person did not know what their account would be, extending the same reckoning scene.
The section's speaker wishes too late for a different life; this next lament wishes that death had been final, making the despair after the account explicit.

The section says people misread abundance and deprivation as honor and humiliation; this ayah calls wealth and children a trial and points to God's greater reward, giving that misreading its correction.
The section recalls how wealth is mistaken for success and then regretted; this ayah describes worldly life as adornment, boasting, and rivalry in wealth before it withers, clarifying what passes.
After 57:20's passing worldly display, this ayah urges racing toward forgiveness and a Garden, a concrete enduring destination related to the section's recognition of the true life.
The section says the dying person finally places “my life” in the right horizon; this ayah names the error as preferring الحياة الدنيا over the lasting life.
Completing 87:16's contrast, this ayah says the Hereafter is better and more enduring, supporting the section's claim that true life is beyond the present one.
The section's stated root ح ي ي covers life through the Hereafter; this ayah directly calls the Hereafter الدار الآخرة and says it is الحياة itself, resolving the meaning of “my life.”
The section distinguishes bodily death from the life that follows; this ayah forbids calling those killed in God's way dead and says they are alive, a direct boundary on what “life” means.
The section's life reaches beyond death; this ayah says those killed in God's way are alive with their Lord and provided for, specifying a continuing life beyond bodily death.

The section's dictionary gloss for root ح ي ي includes the afterlife, and its prose calls that the true life; this ayah contrasts every soul tasting death with receiving its full reward on the Resurrection Day.
The section links the Day of account to the soul's final state; this adjoining passage introduces the one who transgressed before 79:38 names the preference that determines the contrast.
The section's “my life” is finally understood as the lasting one; this ayah identifies the opposing choice as preferring الحياة الدنيا.
After the person who prefers worldly life in 79:38, this ayah names Hell as the refuge, making the consequence of that choice explicit.
The section's closing soul is calm and welcomed; this counterpart describes one who feared standing before the Lord and restrained the soul from desire.
The section's final soul is invited toward its Lord; this next ayah gives the corresponding refuge for the restrained soul as the Garden.
The section labels root ن ف س through the dictionary form التنفس, air leaving the inside; the Qur'an's يَتَنَفَّسَ describes dawn as breathing, a direct image built from that secondary sense.

The section's dictionary entry for root ن ف س identifies the soul as the spirit by which the body lives; this ayah says God takes the souls at death and in sleep, retaining some and releasing others until their term.
The section contrasts a soul invited to return with souls forcibly extracted at death; this ayah's أَخْرِجُوا أَنْفُسَكُمُ and humiliating punishment stage the opposite encounter.
The section's dictionary gloss for root ن ف س is the life-giving spirit; here the angel of death takes the addressed people and they are returned to their Lord, combining departure and return.
The section's settled soul is spoken to gently, unlike a soul taken under force; this ayah describes angels taking people who wronged themselves as they offer submission at death.
The section's tranquil soul is addressed with a return and welcome; here angels take the good in a good state, greet them with peace, and tell them to enter the Garden.
The section explicitly contrasts its tranquil soul with the soul described here; this ayah calls the النفس prone to commanding evil except where the Lord shows mercy.
The section explicitly names this as another state of the soul; the self-reproaching النفس contrasts with the settled soul addressed at the end of 89.
The section's life-giving soul is shown at its bodily limit; this ayah says when it reaches the collarbones, giving a concrete death scene for the soul's departure.
The death scene invoked by the section continues with the question مَنْ رَاقٍ, “who can cure?”, as those present confront the soul's failing body.
Continuing the death scene connected to the section's soul, this ayah says the dying person realizes it is separation, naming what the body is undergoing.
The section describes the soul's departure; this next ayah depicts the legs drawn together in the final bodily moment before the return named in 75:30.
The section says the tranquil soul is told to return to its Lord; this ayah says إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ يَوْمَئِذٍ الْمَسَاقُ, while in the death scene the soul is driven to its Lord.
The section's addressed soul is settled; this ayah also names the النفس but describes its formation, beginning a passage that distinguishes its corrupt and purified outcomes.
The section contrasts a tranquil soul with souls in turmoil; this continuation says the soul is inspired with its wickedness and piety, the two possibilities behind that contrast.
The section's final soul is welcomed; this ayah says the one who purifies the soul succeeds, giving the positive counterpart to the soul states named in the section.
Completing 91:9's contrast, this ayah says the one who corrupts the soul fails, a contrary outcome to the section's tranquil soul.
The section's final النفس المطْمَئِنَّة is a soul at rest; this ayah says hearts find rest in God's remembrance, giving a specific Qur'anic relation between remembrance and inward calm.

The section cites 44:13's question about remembrance after a clear messenger; this nearby ayah has the people ask for the punishment to be removed because they believe, a concrete plea made under the crisis.

After the plea in 44:12 and the messenger rejection in 44:14, this ayah says the punishment will be lifted briefly but they will return to their former course, showing how a reprieve can still be squandered.

The section cites 34:52's failed reach from a distant place; this immediately preceding ayah depicts the terrified people seized from a nearby place with no escape, sharpening the distance and lateness of their grasp.
The section connects 79:35's belated recollection to the great calamity; this next ayah says Hell is exposed for whoever sees, completing the Judgment scene that provokes the memory.

The section ties remembrance and the soul's life to 59:18; this next ayah warns against those who forgot God and were made to forget themselves, a specific opposite to the person's belated return to what their life meant.
The section follows the soul from its bodily life toward return and accounting; this ayah says the death one flees will meet them, then they will be returned to God and told what they did.

The section's person wishes too late that they had sent righteous work ahead; here the people in the Fire ask to be brought out to do good differently, and are reminded that they had time to remember and a warner came.

The section portrays a wish for more time after the final event; this warning says wrongdoers will ask their Lord for a short delay so they can respond and follow the messengers, a concrete version of that impossible postponement.
The section's human recognizes too late what should have been done; this ayah says that when the Hour comes suddenly, people lament what they neglected, matching the same sudden arrival and regret.
The section links the arrival of punishment with belated remembrance; this ayah says those who did wrong conceal regret when they see the punishment, tying the vision of the outcome to remorse.

The section's stated root ق د م describes good work as provision sent ahead; this ayah says whatever good people send ahead for themselves they will find with God, completing the forward-then-arrive relation.

The section's dictionary gloss for root ن ف س concerns the living soul, and it describes souls taken in sleep and death; this ayah says God takes people at night and raises them again by day, adding the recurring sleep-and-return scene.
The section contrasts its tranquil soul with a forced departure; this ayah depicts angels taking the disbelievers' souls while striking their faces and backs, another specific opposite death scene.

The section's tranquil soul is addressed and welcomed toward the Garden; here angels descend on those who remained steadfast and tell them not to fear or grieve, but to rejoice in the promised Garden.
The angelic welcome in 41:30 continues here with the promise of companionship in this life and the Hereafter and whatever the souls desire, extending the section's welcome to the returning soul.
This continuation calls the Garden a hospitality from the Forgiving and Merciful, specifying the welcome that follows the angelic reassurance in 41:30.
The section's late review of a person's life is staged in a Judgment sequence; this ayah says the records are opened before Hell is kindled and every soul knows what it brought.
The section's wish concerns what a person sent ahead for their life; this ayah says each person's record will be brought out on the Resurrection Day, making the life review an individual record.
After the record is brought out in 17:13, this ayah tells each person to read their book and serve as their own reckoner, a direct image of confronting what one has done.
The section says people mistake worldly ease for honor and realize the truth too late; this ayah describes a person who had been joyful among his family before the reckoning.
The family ease in 84:13 is followed by the person's belief that he would never return; this supplies the mistaken view of the afterlife that the section's late regret overturns.
This reply to the person who thought he would not return says his Lord had always seen him, completing the passage's correction of that false security.
